newsitem.title: MOZAMBIQUE: Mozambique may get iron plant instead of S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Mozambique may get iron plant instead of S.Africa.

text.p: An iron ore reduction plant originally set to be built in South Africa is now likely to be situated in southern Mozambique, a senior Mozambique official said on Friday.

The initial plan, announced last August, was to build the facility in South Africa, which has the ore, and use natural gas from Mozambique's Pande gas field, transported through a 900 km pipeline to South Africa, for the ore's reduction.
But Arsenio Mabote, Mozambique's national director for coal and hydrocarbons, told Reuters that the most likely location for the plant would be Mozambique.

"There is a feasibility study to see whether the iron ore reduction plant will be located in Phalaborwa in South Africa or in Mozambique. The way it is now, it looks like the feasibility study indicates that the best option would be to locate the iron ore plant in Maputo," Mabote said.
But he added that siting the plant in Mozambique did not mean the planned 900 km pipeline to South Africa had been cancelled.
"We believe that in Pande there is an upside potential, meaning that we could have excess gas that could be supplied to eventual customers in South Africa," Mabote said.
He said that a plant in Maputo would be an anchor customer for the Pande gas.
The project, in principle, provides for a slurry pipeline to be built from Phalaborwa to Maputo to transport the iron ore to the plant, Mabote said.

Gas from Pande, 700 km north of Maputo, is vital to the project. Last August a statement from the three partners estimated that Pande had "an estimated two trillion cubic feet of proven and recoverable gas reserves".
The three partners in the project are the Mozambican National Hydrocarbons Company (ENC), Enron Corp and South Africa's Industrial Development Corporation (IDC).

Senior Enron executive Peter Wilt said in November 1995 that the project would involve an estimated $700 million investment from various sources for the projected 900 km pipeline and production facilities.
Mabote said the feasibility studies into the plant's site and construction were likely to be completed by the end of 1998.

"For Mozambique it (locating the plant there) would be very beneficial in the sense that it would lead Mozambique to economic growth and would create jobs and more opportunities for regional development," he said.
Mozambique and South Africa are negotiating a bilateral gas trade agreement which is likely to be signed in the next couple of months.
